topic: Craik & Lockhart (1972) / Craik & Tulving (1975): Why Deep Meaning Triples Memory Without Even Trying to Memorize
visual_mode_reason: Fergus Craik and Robert Lockhart's 1972 Levels of Processing framework (tested quantitatively in Craik & Tulving's 1975 10-experiment surprise recall bombshell: ~15% shallow uppercase check vs ~45% rhyme check vs ~80%+ deep sentence-meaning check!) links behavioral encoding depth directly to left inferior prefrontal + hippocampal binding.

primary_case.title: Fergus I. M. Craik & Robert S. Lockhart's 1972 Levels of Processing & Craik & Endel Tulving's 1975 Toronto 10-Experiment Proof
primary_case.place: Department of Psychology, University of Toronto, Canada

people.name: Fergus I. M. Craik & Robert S. Lockhart
people.role: University of Toronto cognitive psychologists whose 1972 paper overturned the idea that repeating words over and over automatically transfers them into long-term memory.

people.name: Endel Tulving
people.role: Co-author with Craik on the classic 1975 Journal of Experimental Psychology: General 10-experiment series measuring 200-ms encoding questions against surprise memory

people.name: John D. E. Gabrieli & Anthony D. Wagner
people.role: Stanford/MIT neuroscientists whose 1998 Science 'Subsequent Memory' fMRI studies watched left inferior prefrontal + parahippocampal activation during deep encoding predict word-by-word which items you will remember.

core_facts.fact: Before 1972, students and textbooks believed a seductive lie: keep a word spinning inside Short-Term Memory long enough by repeating it over and over, and it automatically 'transfers' into permanent Long-Term Memory.

At the University of Toronto in **1972 (*JVLVB*)**, **Fergus Craik and Robert Lockhart** demolished that pipeline myth: memory durability is NOT determined by *which box* an item sits in or *how many times* you mutter it (**Type I Maintenance Rehearsal**), it is a direct byproduct of **HOW DEEPLY you process its meaning** (**Type II Elaborative Processing**).

In **Craik & Watkins (1973, SRC2)**, holding a target word in mind by repeating it mechanically for **12 seconds vs 2 seconds** produced **0% difference** on a surprise final memory test — mechanical repetition without meaning left virtually zero deeper trace.

Then **Craik & Tulving (1975, 10 experiments!)** flashed words for **200 milliseconds** with NO warning of a memory test (**incidental learning!**), asking one of THREE quick yes/no questions per word: (1) **Shallow Structural**: *'Is the word in CAPITAL LETTERS?'* (`TABLE`), (2) **Intermediate Phonemic**: *'Does the word RHYME with weight?'* (`crate`), or (3) **Deep Semantic**: *'Does the word fit: The girl placed the ___ on the table?'* (`watch`).

On a **surprise recognition/recall test** minutes later, memory skyrocketed **3x to 5x** solely from which question the brain answered for half a second: **~15–18% recognized after Case check to ~45–50% after Rhyme check to ~80–90%+ after Deep Meaning check**.

Even more shocking (Hyde & Jenkins; Craik & Tulving 1975): volunteers who were **NOT even trying to memorize** while answering Deep Semantic questions **beat or tied volunteers told 'Try as hard as you can to memorize this list for a test!'** — proving **WHAT you think about** crushes **wanting to remember**.

Critics rightly asked: *'Wait — what if the final test asks for RHYMES instead of words?'* **Morris, Bransford & Franks (1977, SRC5)** proved **Transfer-Appropriate Processing**: rhyme encoding actually beats semantic encoding ONLY on a rhyme-matching test, though across 99% of real life and exams we retrieve by *meaning*.

In **1998 (*Science*)**, Wagner, Brewer, Gabrieli, and colleagues scanned volunteers in event-related fMRI during shallow case vs deep semantic questions: trial-by-trial surges in **left ventrolateral prefrontal cortex** and **left parahippocampal/hippocampal cortex** predicted *before the test even happened* which exact words each human would remember or forget.

In Craik and Tulving (1975), answering a deep semantic sentence-fit question took roughly 0.5 to 0.8 seconds (about half a second to 800 milliseconds) yet boosted later word recognition from 17% (case check) to 82%.

In Craik and Tulving's (1975) incidental encoding experiments, unexpected recognition climbed from ~17% after shallow letter-case judgments to ~48% after rhyme judgments and ~82% after 20-second semantic sentence-fit judgments.

wow_facts.fact: Flash the exact same word for **one-fifth of a second** with zero warning of a quiz: ask *'Is it in ALL CAPS?'* and **83% of people forget it**; ask *'Would it fit inside a teacup?'* and **over 80% remember it effortlessly**.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Half a second of meaning beats ten minutes of robotic staring.

wow_facts.fact: Tell Group A *'There WILL be a huge memory test — try your hardest to memorize!'* while checking letter shapes, and tell Group B *'No test at all — just rate how pleasant each word is!'* — **Group B crushes the intentional memorizers**.
wow_facts.why_surprising: 'Intent to remember' does almost nothing; *depth of thought* does everything.

wow_facts.fact: Ever wondered why **Americans could NOT draw the front of a U.S. one-cent piece from memory** (Nickerson & Adams 1979) despite touching it **thousands of times**? Because you only ever process its *shallow copper color* to separate it from silver change — zero deep processing = zero detail memory.
wow_facts.why_surprising: 10,000 shallow glances lose to 1 deep question.

wow_facts.fact: Inside an fMRI scanner (Wagner & Gabrieli 1998), neuroscientists can literally watch **left inferior frontal + hippocampal cortex** light up on a single word and predict *'She's going to remember #14 and forget #15!'* hours before the test.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Levels of Processing visible word by word inside the living brain.

misconceptions.myth: Highlighting textbook sentences in yellow and re-reading notes five times puts knowledge into long-term memory.
misconceptions.truth: Passive re-reading and highlighting are classic **Type I shallow maintenance** — they create cozy visual familiarity while producing dismal exam recall compared with asking 'Why is this true and how does it connect to X?'.

misconceptions.myth: Trying really hard and gritting your teeth ('I MUST remember this!') flips on a memory switch.
misconceptions.truth: Human brains have NO direct 'Save to Disk' willpower button; memory is the automatic residue of deep semantic elaboration.

misconceptions.myth: 'Deep processing' just means spending more seconds staring at the word.
misconceptions.truth: Craik & Tulving (1975 Experiment 5!) invented a tricky shallow task (*'Does this word follow Consonant-Vowel-Consonant-Consonant-Vowel pattern?'*) that took **LONGER** (1.7 seconds!) than a quick 0.8-second meaning question — and **fast Deep Meaning STILL crushed slow Shallow Letter-Counting**.

everyday_hooks: Reading an entire page of a textbook twice at 11 p.m. while thinking about snacks — shallow font-scanning with 0% semantic encoding.
Meeting someone at a conference, repeating their name mechanically twice, and forgetting it 30 seconds later vs linking their name to a vivid question or trait.
Swapping passive re-reading for 3 'Why / How does this compare to...' questions and cutting study time in half.
